periods.activity_title: First Encounter — Read-Aloud and Choral Reading

time_bands.activity: Teacher introduces the poem's title and invites students to share what they know about Gilli Danda. A quick paired exchange surfaces prior experiences of outdoor play.
Teacher reads the poem aloud with expression, pausing after each stanza to let the rhythm settle. Students follow in their textbooks (pp.79–80).
Class moves into choral reading — the whole poem read together twice, then stanza by stanza in groups, with the teacher conducting pace and volume.
Teacher poses two open questions aloud — 'What feeling does this poem give you?' and 'Which image did you see most clearly in your mind?' — and takes a few quick spoken responses from volunteers.

periods.teacher_notes: The poem's short, punchy lines and internal rhyme make the choral reading energetic; slow the group down for the third stanza so the imagery of the gilli flying under bright blue skies lands clearly. Resist moving to questions this sitting — the full-text encounter is the whole purpose.

periods.activity_title: Comprehension Discussion — Making Meaning of the Poem

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us Think — A. (p.80): questions 1–4, discuss what the poem says about the game, feelings, and setting.

homework.task_brief: Let us Think — A. (p.80): answer questions 5 and 6 in writing — meaning of 'sound' and the word showing happiness.

time_bands.activity: Teacher leads a brief re-recite of the poem's opening stanza together before opening the discussion, anchoring the words fresh in students' minds.

Let us Think — A., questions 1 and 2 (p.80): teacher asks which game the poem names and what equipment it needs, then how players feel while playing. Students respond in full spoken sentences; teacher probes with 'What word in the poem tells you that?'

Let us Think — A., questions 3 and 4 (p.80): class discusses what happens to the gilli when struck, then identifies specific lines that place the game outdoors. Teacher writes key phrases on the board as evidence.
Pairs share their favourite outdoor-setting image from the poem; two or three pairs report back to the class. Teacher draws the discussion to a close by highlighting the poem's movement imagery.

periods.teacher_notes: Questions 1–4 move from literal recall toward inference; keep students pointing to specific lines as evidence rather than answering from general knowledge. Questions 5 and 6 require the children to think about word meaning and will be more productive as written homework after this oral grounding.

periods.activity_title: Think and Discuss — Outdoor Play and Imagination

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us Think + Let us Speak + Let us Listen (p.80): Think and Discuss prompts 1–3 — outdoor play preferences, five favourite games, imagining as the gilli.

time_bands.activity: Teacher introduces the three discussion prompts from the textbook (p.80) and models the first response briefly — sharing her own experience of an outdoor game to demonstrate the expected register.
Prompt 1 — 'Do you enjoy playing outdoors? Why or why not?' Students talk in pairs, then four or five individuals share with the class. Teacher notes varied reasons on the board.

Prompt 2 — 'Name five outdoor games you enjoy with friends.' Students call out games; teacher builds a class list on the board. Students then use the list to construct two or three full spoken sentences about their favourite.

Prompt 3 — 'Imagine you are the small gilli flying into the sky.' Students close their eyes for thirty seconds of silent imagining, then share what they would see in two or three spoken sentences. Teacher prompts with 'What colours? What sounds? What would be below you?'

periods.teacher_notes: The third prompt is imaginative and calls on the poem's sky imagery — golden sun, bright blue — so encourage students to borrow that language. Prompt 2 naturally surfaces a variety of traditional and modern games; celebrate both without directing children toward any one answer.

periods.activity_title: Let us Speak — Presenting a Group Game

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us Think + Let us Speak + Let us Listen (p.80): Let us Speak — short oral presentation on a group game of the student's choice.

time_bands.activity: Teacher models a short oral presentation about one game — covering its name, indoor/outdoor nature, number of players, equipment, and a key rule — so students hear the expected structure before preparing their own.

Students work individually to organise their thoughts on a game of their choice, using the five-point structure from the textbook prompt (p.80). Teacher circulates and prompts those who are stuck with questions like 'How many players do you need?'
Five or six volunteers deliver their short presentations to the class. After each, the class asks one clarifying question. Teacher gives brief spoken feedback on clarity and completeness.
Teacher highlights two or three strong features heard across the presentations — clear rules, vivid equipment descriptions — and invites the class to name the game they most want to try.

periods.teacher_notes: Students often describe familiar games but struggle to state the rules precisely; prompt them during preparation with 'What is not allowed?' to get at the rules dimension. Keep individual presentations brief so multiple students have a turn.

periods.activity_title: Let us Listen — Action-Response Listening Activity

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us Think + Let us Speak + Let us Listen (p.80): Let us Listen — teacher reads phrases aloud; students respond with matching actions.

time_bands.activity: Teacher explains the activity: she will read a phrase from the poem aloud and students must listen carefully and perform the matching action without speaking. A quick demonstration of the first action sets expectations.

Teacher reads each of the four phrases — 'Swing and hit', 'Watch it go!', 'Laughing, playing', 'Shade your eyes from the sun' — three to four times each at varied pace. Students perform the matching action each time and freeze when the teacher pauses.
Pairs take turns — one says a phrase, the other performs the action, then they swap. This builds both listening accuracy and spoken fluency with the poem's language.

Class returns to a full-group round: teacher calls phrases in random order and students respond together, then individually at speed. Teacher closes by asking which phrase felt most like the game — a brief spoken share-out.

periods.teacher_notes: Vary the pace deliberately — a quick run followed by a slow, deliberate reading — so students are genuinely listening rather than anticipating. The activity connects the poem's physical imagery to the body, reinforcing the energetic, communal tone the poem celebrates.

periods.activity_title: Prefixes — Un- and Re-: Making New Words

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us Learn — A. (p.81): add 'un-' or 're-' to five base words and write each new word with its meaning.

time_bands.activity: Teacher writes 'unhappy' and 'redo' on the board and elicits from students what changed when the prefix was added. The concepts 'un- = not' and 're- = again' are established with two or three further quick examples from everyday language.

Let us Learn — A. (p.81): students work through the five base words — write, aware, comfortable, arrange, think — choosing the correct prefix, writing the new word and its meaning. Teacher circulates and checks that 'rewrite' and 'rearrange' are handled alongside 'unaware', 'uncomfortable', and 'rethink'.

Whole-class check: teacher reveals answers one by one, asking different students to read their new word aloud and give its meaning in a sentence. The class decides together which prefix fits each base word and why.

Quick word-building extension: teacher asks students to think of one more word that takes 'un-' and one more that takes 're-' from their own vocabulary; two or three volunteers share and the class confirms whether the prefix works.

periods.teacher_notes: Students frequently confuse 'reaware' (non-word) with 'unaware'; drawing attention to whether the base word already begins with a vowel sound helps. The textbook's Sameer example grounds the concept in a relatable context — refer back to it if students lose track of why prefixes matter.

periods.activity_title: Abstract and Concrete Nouns — Sorting the Grid

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us Learn — B. (p.82): encircle concrete nouns in the word grid; identify remaining words as abstract nouns; add examples of one's own.

time_bands.activity: Teacher introduces the distinction between concrete and abstract nouns through a quick demonstration: she holds up a pencil (concrete — you can touch it) and then writes 'joy' on the board (abstract — you feel it but cannot hold it). Students offer one or two examples of each from their own experience.

Let us Learn — B. (p.82): students work with the word grid, encircling every noun they can see, taste, touch, or smell. Teacher circulates, pausing at 'truth', 'lie', 'happiness', and 'fear' to ask students 'Can you pick this up?' as a self-check.
Whole-class review: teacher reads across the grid row by row; students call out 'concrete' or 'abstract'. Any disagreements are debated briefly with the 'Can you sense it physically?' test.

Students write two abstract nouns of their own choosing in their notebooks and share with a partner. Three or four pairs share their choices with the class; teacher adds interesting examples to the board.

periods.teacher_notes: Words such as 'chessboard' and 'football' are physical and often correctly identified; 'happiness' and 'fear' are the productive sticking points. Drawing a quick two-column chart on the board — CONCRETE | ABSTRACT — lets students see the distribution at a glance as the review progresses.

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us Learn — C. (p.83): fill in blanks with the correct possessive pronoun from the given list.

time_bands.activity: Teacher places six classroom objects on a desk and names their owners, then forms a sentence about each using a possessive pronoun — 'This pencil is mine', 'The ruler is his', and so on — writing each pronoun on the board as it is used.

Let us Learn — C. (p.83): students work through all six sentences, selecting the correct possessive pronoun from the box — mine, yours, his, hers, ours, theirs. Teacher circulates, helping students identify the noun and its owner before choosing.

Whole-class check sentence by sentence: teacher reads the sentence aloud with a pause at the blank; class chorus the answer. For any disagreements, the teacher restates the ownership clue ('belongs to her') to guide correction.
Students write two original sentences of their own using any two possessive pronouns from the list. Three or four share their sentences aloud; class confirms correct usage.

periods.teacher_notes: The pronoun 'theirs' (sentence 3, cousins) is the most reliably confused, as students often default to 'their'; draw attention to the absence of a noun following the pronoun in each answer position. The concrete classroom-object demonstration at the opening reduces abstraction significantly.

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us Write — A. (p.85): find dictionary meanings for five poem words and write an original sentence for each.

homework.task_brief: Let us Write — B. (p.85): rearrange four scrambled word groups — 'are cows where the', 'is your house which', 'it time is what', 'the blue why sky is' — into correct questions and write them in the notebook.

time_bands.activity: Teacher models the task with the word 'playground': looks it up in the dictionary, reads the definition aloud, then writes a sentence on the board that uses the word meaningfully. Students see the two-step process — find meaning, then use it.

Let us Write — A. (p.85): students use their dictionaries to find meanings for 'quit', 'gather', 'swing', 'underneath', and 'golden'. Teacher circulates to check that students are reading full dictionary entries, not just the first listed meaning.

Students write one original sentence for each of the five words in their notebooks. Teacher prompts those who are stuck to think of a context from the poem — swinging a danda, gathering under golden sunlight — as a starting image.
Three or four students read their sentences aloud. Class gives a thumbs-up if the word is used in a way that matches the dictionary meaning. Teacher gives brief spoken feedback.

periods.teacher_notes: Students often write sentences that demonstrate the word's spelling but not its meaning; the thumbs-up peer-check at the close addresses this. Encourage sentences that are specific and personal rather than generic — a sentence using 'gather' that names a real place or event is richer than 'We gather together'.

periods.activity_title: Antonyms in Context — Finding the Odd Word Out

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us Write — D. (p.87): circle the word different in meaning from the underlined word in each sentence; complete all eight items independently.

time_bands.activity: Teacher works through one example on the board — the word 'expensive' — asking students to decide which of the three options means the opposite rather than the same thing. The class establishes the strategy: find the underlined word's meaning, then eliminate the synonyms.
Let us Write — D. (p.87): students work independently through all eight sentences, circling the word that differs in meaning from the underlined word. Teacher circulates quietly.

Whole-class review: teacher reads each sentence; students call out their answer and justify briefly — 'expensive means costly, so cheap is different because it means the opposite'. Teacher confirms or corrects.
Teacher asks students which pair of words they found most surprising — the underlined word and its odd one out — and takes two or three spoken responses, consolidating vocabulary understanding.

periods.teacher_notes: Items 6 and 7 — 'nervously / confidently' and 'vibrant / dull' — typically provoke the most debate; make sure students are comparing against the underlined word, not against each other's options. This task builds antonym awareness in a sentence context, which is more durable than isolated word lists.

periods.activity_title: Spellathon Word Wheel and the Riddle

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us Do + Just for Fun — B. (p.90): Spellathon letter wheel — make words of three or more letters; attempt the seven-letter word.
Let us Do + Just for Fun (p.90): Just for Fun riddle — solve and discuss the answer.

time_bands.activity: Teacher introduces the Spellathon letter wheel (p.90) — letters A, C, E, T, H, E, R — and reads the rules aloud. The example words 'tea' and 'reach' are noted on the board so the format is clear.

Let us Do + Just for Fun — B. (p.90): students work individually to list as many three-or-more-letter words as they can from the wheel letters. Teacher circulates, prompting students who are stuck by asking 'Can you find a word starting with CH?' or 'What about a word ending in -ER?'

Class pools words: teacher goes around the room collecting one word per student and writes them on the board without repeating. The class together tries to identify the seven-letter word using all letters — 'teacher' — and celebrates if any student found it independently.

Just for Fun (p.90): teacher reads the riddle aloud — 'It belongs to you, but your friends use it more than you. What is it?' — and gives students a minute of silent thinking. Several answers are shared; the agreed answer is discussed and students explain why it works as a riddle.

periods.teacher_notes: The seven-letter answer 'teacher' delights most classes when they arrive at it; hold it back until the pooling stage so the discovery happens together. The riddle's answer — 'your name' — is worth a brief conversation about what makes a riddle satisfying: the surprise of a familiar thing reframed.

items.item_stem: Read the lines beginning “The small gilli, up high it flies” on page 79. Which two features of the outdoor setting are described in that stanza?

options.label: A
options.text: A playground fence and tall trees

options.label: B
options.text: Bright blue skies and golden rays of the sun

options.label: C
options.text: Green grass and a flowing river

options.label: D
options.text: White clouds and a silver moon

what_each_option_reveals.C: The student may be drawing on a general outdoor scene rather than reading the poem’s specific imagery.
what_each_option_reveals.D: The student may be associating ‘sky’ with night imagery rather than the sunny daytime scene the poem describes.
what_each_option_reveals.A: The student may be picturing a generic playground without attending to the poem’s descriptive language.

items.item_stem: The poem says the players “never quit.” In your own words, explain what feeling or quality this line shows about the children who play Gilli Danda.

teacher_guide.suggested_answer: The line shows that the children are determined and enthusiastic — they keep playing and do not give up, which reflects the joyful, energetic spirit the poem celebrates.

items.item_stem: Your teacher will read the phrase ‘Watch it go!’ from the poem aloud. Which action matches what a player does at that moment in Gilli Danda?

options.text: The player bends down to pick up the gilli from the ground.
The player covers their ears to block out the sound of the hit.
The player raises their arms and looks upward to follow the gilli’s flight.

teacher_guide.suggested_answer: Statement 1 is true: the player raises their arms and watches upward as the gilli flies through the air after being struck. Statements 2 and 3 describe actions that do not match the moment of watching the gilli go.

items.item_stem:
Choose the word that is most nearly opposite in meaning to the underlined word.

The children gathered in the playground to play Gilli Danda.

what_each_option_reveals.C: The student may be thinking of a related playground action rather than the meaning of ‘gathered’.
what_each_option_reveals.A: The student may recognise ‘crowded’ as similar to gathering rather than opposite.
what_each_option_reveals.B: The student may associate ‘joined’ with coming together, which is close in meaning to ‘gathered’ rather than opposite.
